p78: 78.  As to the concluding hearing, the Government explained that the applicant and his lawyer had both been present at the beginning of the hearing, but that while it was in progress the applicant had done nothing but rant and shout. The presiding judge had warned him twice and it was only after finding that this had had no effect that he had ordered his removal from the courtroom.
p79: 79.  His removal had therefore been a measure of last resort, taken by the presiding judge in order to maintain order in the courtroom.
p80: 80.  The Government further submitted that, had the applicant wished to confess or show remorse, he would have had ample opportunity to do so during the trial.
p81: 81.  They added that by the time the applicant was removed from the courtroom, all the evidence had already been taken.
p82: 82.  Lastly, they pointed out that the applicant’s lawyer had remained in the courtroom and had been able to present his closing arguments.
p83: 83.  In view of the above considerations, the Government considered that the applicant’s right to defend himself in person or through legal assistance had not been restricted in any way.
p84: 84.  The relevant parts of the Chamber’s assessment read as follows:
p85: 85.  The mere fact that a trial judge has already taken decisions concerning the same offence cannot be held as in itself justifying fears as to his impartiality (see Hauschildt v. Denmark, 24 May 1989, § 50, Series A no. 154, and Romero Martin v. Spain (dec.), no. 32045/03, 12 June 2006, concerning pre-trial decisions; Ringeisen v. Austria, 16 July 1971, § 97, Series A no. 13; Diennet v. France, 26 September 1995, § 38, Series A no. 325-A; and Vaillant v. France, no. 30609/04, §§ 29-35, 18 December 2008, concerning situations where a case has been remitted for re-examination after a decision had been reversed or quashed by a higher court; Thomann v. Switzerland, 10 June 1996, §§ 35-36, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-III, concerning the retrial of a defendant convicted in absentia; and Craxi III v. Italy (dec.), no. 63226/00, 14 June 2001, and Ferrantelli and Santangelo, cited above, § 59, concerning situations where judges had participated in proceedings against co-accused of the applicants).
p86: 86.  In the Court’s view, no legitimate reason to fear a lack of impartiality can be found in the fact that the same judge took part in the adoption of a decision at first instance and then participated in the proceedings which followed the remittal of the case for re-examination after that decision had been quashed. It cannot be stated as a general rule resulting from the obligation to be impartial that a superior court which sets aside a judicial decision is bound to send the case back to a differently composed bench of the lower court (see Ringeisen, cited above, § 97).
p87: 87.  The present case does not concern a situation where the first decision was quashed and the case remitted for retrial following an ordinary appeal; in the instant case a fresh indictment was issued against the applicant in respect of partly identical charges. However, the Court considers that the principles set out in paragraph 85 above are equally applicable in the present case. The mere fact that Judge M.K. took part both in the criminal proceedings conducted before the Osijek County Court under number K-4/97 and in the criminal proceedings against the applicant before the same court under number K-33/06 should not be considered as in itself incompatible with the requirement of impartiality under Article 6 of the Convention. Moreover, in the first proceedings Judge M.K. did not adopt a judgment finding the applicant guilty or innocent, and at no point did he engage in an assessment of evidence relevant to a decision on that question (see paragraph 17 above). He confined himself to examining whether the conditions for the application of the General Amnesty Act were satisfied in the applicant’s case.
